title: Will Getting Rid Of Admissions Tests Make Selective Schools More Equitable?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler asks whether dropping admissions tests at selective schools will really deliver equity. She accepts that the racial imbalance at elite schools is unfair, but argues that test scores reflect academic knowledge and vocabulary that affluent students pick up more easily outside school. Because those gaps widen with grade level, abandoning tests treats a symptom. She evaluates several proposals, doubting that the Ivy League can remediate large knowledge gaps and warning that selective high schools will still need tutoring and writing instruction. Her central claim is that the most equitable move is a content-rich elementary curriculum in social studies, science, literature and the arts, with reading tests tied to what children have been taught.
points: Reading tests largely measure background knowledge and academic vocabulary, which is why they predict school success.
Knowledge gaps widen with each grade, so remediation is hardest at college and high school levels.
Grades and recommendations vary with the school environment and are not a neutral replacement for tests.
The overlooked equity lever is rich elementary content in history, science, literature and the arts.
Removing tests or the phrase achievement gap no more fixes the problem than abandoning Covid tests ends the disease.
quotes: They don’t try to assess whether kids have learned whatever content they’ve been taught. Instead, they aim to measure general reading comprehension skills.
The more you know, the better your chances of understanding a passage on a test and answering the questions correctly.

In our current system, gaps in academic knowledge—which are reflected in test scores—grow larger and harder to narrow as grade levels go up. By the time students reach high school, they’re often huge.
But it’s tremendously difficult to compensate for large knowledge gaps at the college level, and there’s no reason to believe that Ivy League schools would do a better job than community colleges.

By far the most equitable move that any school district could make is one that isn’t being discussed: change the elementary curriculum so that it provides all children with rich content in social studies, science, literature and the arts, building their academic knowledge and vocabulary.
But the cause of that discrepancy isn’t testing—it’s our standard approach to teaching, which simply doesn’t work for most kids.
